title: Artificial Lawns in Myrtle Beach | TIMELESS Grass & Greens
description: Artificial lawns sized to North Myrtle Beach and Myrtle Beach coverage limits, Myrtle Beach tree rules and North Carolina’s turf exclusion. Free visit.
h1: An artificial lawn sized to what your lot is allowed to cover.
lede: Skip the mowing on a lawn planned for your lot, anywhere from Shallotte to Burgess. A lawn usually covers more ground than a dog run or a putting green, so how your city counts it matters. We measure the yard and check the ground at a free visit, then draw a custom layout you approve before work starts.
wins: Size the lawn to your district’s coverage limit
Keep the city’s protected trees out of the dig
Approve the layout before work starts

answer.question: What should I check before replacing my Grand Strand lawn with turf?
answer.answer: Start with how your city counts it. In North Myrtle Beach, an R-1 lot can be no more than 40 percent impervious, and a surface that misses the city’s pervious test counts toward that limit. In Myrtle Beach’s single-family districts, 50 percent of the lot must stay pervious, and the code counts stone, shell or gravel surfacing as impervious. In Brunswick County, North Carolina law leaves qualifying turf out of built-upon area. Call 303-349-2368 for a free estimate.

blocks.h2: Find your district’s limit before you size the lawn.
paras: North Myrtle Beach sets its hard-surface limits district by district. Sec. 23-18 says no more than 40 percent of an R-1 lot may be impervious, and 45 percent in R-1A. For a single-family house, the district tables allow 50 percent in R-1B (Sec. 23-18.1) and 60 percent in R-2B (Sec. 23-20.1). Those are the limits in the city code version of 23 July 2026. Ask the city which district your lot is in.

A turf lawn stays off that count only if it passes Sec. 23-129.4, which covers single-family and duplex lots not subject to site-specific development plan review. A surface that misses its pervious test counts as impervious, regardless of material type or labeling. The test came in with Ord. No. 25-45 on 6 October 2025, and our North Myrtle Beach page lists each part of it. The pool basin is left out of the count, but the deck around it is not.

When council passed it on second reading, city staff said the ordinance required the manufacturer’s certification sheet with the permit application, and that it “would only affect permits if the 40 percent pervious ratio was exceeded” (council minutes, 6 October 2025). So add up the house, driveway, patio and pool deck before you size the lawn. If the total stays under your limit with the lawn counted as hard surface, ask the city to confirm the lawn needs no pervious review. If it goes over, the turf and base have to pass the test, and you are responsible for keeping the system infiltrating over time.

blocks.h2: Keep half the lot pervious, and ask how the base counts.
paras: Inside Myrtle Beach city limits, the dimensional table in Section 1603 sets a minimum pervious surface of 50% in the R-5, R-7, R-8, R-10 and R-15 single-family districts (zoning code current through 16 February 2026). Grass is part of that pervious half. Replace it, and what matters is whether the city still counts the new lawn on the pervious side.

The code doesn’t say how turf counts. The definitions in Sec. 203 never mention it. They measure a surface against how fast vegetation-bearing soil absorbs water, and they list “stone, shell or gravel surfacing” among the items counted as impervious lot coverage. Landscaped open space means lawns, shrubs, trees or other vegetation and permeable ground cover capable of absorbing runoff water. Turf goes down over a base, so ask about the base as well as the turf.

Before you size the lawn, ask Myrtle Beach Planning and Zoning in writing how the turf and its base count toward your district’s pervious minimum. Take the turf’s product sheet and a drawing of the base with you. Our Myrtle Beach page explains the two kinds of ground under the city, which shape that base.

blocks.h2: Taking out the grass is more than mowing.
paras: Section 903.L of the Myrtle Beach zoning code says a clearing/grubbing permit from the Construction Services Department must be obtained before any site clearing or vegetation alteration, other than mowing. Applications for clearing, grubbing or grading include a tree protection zone plan, and grading, filling, ditching and storage inside that zone are prohibited.

On a lot with one single-family house, the zone protects significant and landmark trees. Significant trees are live oak, white oak, eastern red cedar, southern magnolia and bald cypress measuring 4 inches or more in diameter at breast height. Landmark trees are listed species at or above a set diameter, such as a live oak of 25 inches.

Ask Construction Services whether removing your lawn needs that permit before work is scheduled. At the free visit, show us each of those trees near the lawn, so the layout leaves room for the protection zone the city asks for.

blocks.h2: Across the state line, the whole installation has to qualify.
paras: In Shallotte, Carolina Shores and the rest of Brunswick County, G.S. 143-214.7D says that for State or local stormwater programs, artificial turf is not built-upon area when it is manufactured to let water drain through its backing and installed to the manufacturer’s specifications over a pervious surface. Except as specifically required by federal law, a local government may not enforce a definition of built-upon area that doesn’t comply. A property owner or developer may also opt out of the exclusion (statute text read 12 September 2026).

The exclusion depends on how the turf is made and how it goes in. Keep the product sheet that shows the backing drains and a drawing of the base under it, then ask the town or county reviewer to confirm in writing how the finished lawn counts. Our state-line guide covers where local codes stand and turf near the water, and our Shallotte page explains how to confirm which office reviews your parcel.

faq.q: Does North Myrtle Beach need a soil test on my lot?
faq.a: Not under the current code. Sec. 23-129.4 says its pervious standard applies regardless of native soil conditions, and site-specific soil testing is not required. The surface still has to show two inches an hour on manufacturer testing or accepted industry standards, and the permit is subject to inspection. We still check your ground at the free visit, because the base has to suit it.

faq.q: My lot is outside city limits. Do these limits apply?
faq.a: Not the city tables above. For a lot in unincorporated Horry County, give the county your address and the whole scope, including digging, the base and any grading, and ask what applies. Show us swales, drains and pond edges at the free visit so the lawn doesn’t block the way water leaves. Our Carolina Forest and Forestbrook pages cover drainage features and plats.

faq.q: Can my HOA stop an artificial lawn?
faq.a: Its rules can limit one. On the South Carolina side, S.C. Code 27-30-130 says that, except as the section provides otherwise, an association’s governing documents must be recorded in the county where the property is to be enforceable. Ask the board which recorded covenant or rule covers ground cover, send the layout and get the answer in writing. Our HOA article covers what to ask for.

faq.q: Is there a rebate for replacing my lawn with turf?
faq.a: GSWSA’s water conservation page lists none. Its lawn tips are about when and where to water: in the evening or at night, not on windy days, and with sprinklers wetting only the lawn. Confirm with the provider on your water bill before counting on one. Our rebate guide covers what to ask.

faq.q: What should I bring to the free visit?
faq.a: Your address and zoning district if you know it, a survey or plat showing the house, driveway, patio and pool deck, your HOA’s rules, and photos of where water stands after rain. In Myrtle Beach, point out every tree near the lawn, especially oaks, cedars, magnolias and cypresses. Our Grand Strand page lists everywhere we work.
